Vanessa / Marissa —

Quick sizing notes based on Elena's numbers (25 steady, 40 peak concurrent; 1.5k input / 0.8k gen):

Assumptions (conservative):
- Model family: 30B parameter base architecture (32k context support).
- Baseline FP16 model memory (weights in GPU): ~80 GB (including optimizer/overheads)
- KV cache: worst-case per-session KV cache = sequence_length * hidden_size * 2 (key+value) approx ~6–10 GB per long-lived session for 32k context depending on hidden size; assume 8 GB/session for planning.
- Batch packing and continuous batching reduces per-request overhead; assume effective concurrency utilization 70% due to interactivity.

Quantization impacts (rough):
- 8-bit (INT8) / QAT: weights footprint ~45–50% of FP16 => ~36–40 GB
- 4-bit (LLM.int8/awq/qlo style) : weights footprint ~30–35% of FP16 => ~24–28 GB, but requires additional CPU decoding steps and can increase CPU-KV traffic for some runtimes.

Sizing scenarios (targeting <700ms median token latency):
A) Conservative (no quantization, FP16):
- Per-GPU usable model memory: assume A100-80GB with ~72 GB usable after system overhead. One model instance occupies ~80 GB so requires model sharding across 2 GPUs or use A100-160 equivalent (or multi-GPU partitioning). For dedicated pool, recommend 2x A100-80 (NVLink, model parallel) per instance.
- For 40 peak concurrent sessions with KV cache pinned, estimate 40 * 8GB = 320 GB KV memory; KV can be either on-GPU (preferred for latency) or managed with local NVMe-backed KV offload. On-GPU KV requires roughly 5 GPUs worth of memory (assuming 80 GB GPU memory) dedicated to cache; combined with model shards we'd estimate a cluster of 12x A100-80GB to get headroom and 2x redundancy.

B) Balanced (4-bit quant + KV on-GPU with caching):
- Model weights per instance ~28 GB, plus KV cache when on-GPU. We can fit one model instance per A100-80 with room for KV if we use careful memory packing. For 40 sessions, KV = 320 GB; with 80GB per GPU, ~4 GPUs dedicated to KV plus ~6 GPUs for model instances (including headroom and replicas) => 10x A100-80GB recommended.

C) Cost-optimized (4-bit quant + NVMe KV offload):
- Accept slightly higher tail latency for cold contexts with NVMe; plan 8x A100-80GB + fast NVMe pool for KV, with automated hot-spotting of KV into GPU memory for active sessions.

Recommendation for POC: go with Balanced scenario to prove quality tradeoffs while keeping latency in target. Proposed dedicated pool: 10x A100-80GB for 6-week POC with ability to scale to 12 if we observe higher tail latency.

Operational notes / tradeoffs:
- Quantization validation: run representative evaluation suites (short generative prompts + retrieval matches) against unquantized FP16 baseline to measure quality delta. Expect ~1–3% metric delta for instruction-following tasks for well-calibrated 4-bit recipes.
- KV persistence: On-GPU KV gives best latency but increases GPU memory footprint significantly; NVMe offload reduces GPU count but will show higher cold-start latencies.
- Autoscaling: We recommend reserving 80% of pool for POC usage and leave 20% for operational buffer and canary.

I'll prepare a one-page capacity summary and include the numeric assumptions above.

- Karthik
Senior Solutions Architect, Redwood Inference

Vanessa / team —

Adding quantization / eval guidance so procurement has realistic expectations:

Summary guidance:
- 8-bit (INT8 / QAT) is lower-risk for POC: moderate footprint reduction (~45%) with minimal downstream quality impact if you fine-tune or run a short QAT pass on representative prompts. Good first step to reduce GPU requirements with minimal eval overhead.
- 4-bit (LLM.int8/awq/qlo) yields larger footprint reductions (~65–70% of FP16 -> 25–30% of original) but requires careful per-layer recipe tuning and per-task validation. For some biomedical-finetuned models, we have observed a 1–4% loss on factuality/QA F1 depending on the recipe.

Recommended evals for the POC (to be run against all quant levels):
1) Prompt suite of 150 prompts representative of analyst workflows (retrieval + generation). Measure ROUGE/F1 and two human pass/fail checks on 30 sampled responses.
2) Latency and tail (95th) under 25/40 concurrent load patterns.
3) Sanity checks for hallucination on a curated set of 40 known-reference items.

Rollout plan:
- Week 0–1: Deploy FP16 baseline on a small reserved slice for validation.
- Week 2: Deploy INT8 across canary 10% of sessions; run evals and human review.
- Week 3: If quality within threshold (<2% drop), expand to 60% with 4-bit experiments on isolated model variant for comparison.
- Week 4–5: Finalize quant recipe and baseline comparisons; produce sign-off report for procurement.

Attachments: quant-eval-summary.pdf (contains past internal evals vs similar biomedical models; stub).
